description: A creative and motivated team passionate about space science, technology, data visualization, and innovation. We enjoy exploring new ideas, solving real-world problems, and building meaningful, user-friendly prototypes that turn complex concepts into engaging experiences.
summary:
EarthPulse is a browser-based project that turns NASA’s “Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 — EIC Version” visualization into sound.
As a spatial sweep moves across the rendered map, visible patterns become simple tones: lights out maps to a lower pitch, no change to a middle reference pitch, and new lights to a higher pitch. Cells with no signal or an uncertain classification remain silent, so silence is never confused with “no change.”
Users can hear the three reference tones through the Audible Legend, select individual cells to inspect their qualitative classification and play the corresponding tone, and compare the patterns shown in NASA’s India and Ukraine regional insets. The original NASA visualization remains visible throughout the experience.
EarthPulse responds to The Earth Information Jukebox by offering another way to explore Earth data beyond a visual map. It is designed with blind and low-vision users in mind, as well as anyone who wants to experience data through sound. It has not yet been formally tested with blind or low-vision users.
This is a qualitative sonification of a rendered visualization—not a calibrated measurement of radiance, brightness, population or geographic change.
details:
EarthPulse is a browser-based project that turns NASA’s “Change in Night Lights between 2012 and 2023 — EIC Version” visualization into an interactive sound experience.

The project uses the original NASA visualization as its starting point. An offline image-processing pipeline divides the rendered map into a 96 × 27 grid and identifies broad visual patterns such as new lights, no change, lights out, no signal and unknown. When users start the spatial sweep, the application moves across the grid and translates these patterns into sounds. Lights out is represented by a lower pitch, no change by a middle reference pitch, and new lights by a higher pitch. Cells with no reliable signal or an unknown classification remain silent.

Users can first listen to the three reference tones through the Audible Legend. They can then select individual cells on the map, view the cell’s qualitative classification in the Prove It panel and play its corresponding tone using Play This Value. The project also includes a qualitative comparison of the visual patterns in NASA’s India and Ukraine regional insets. Unknown and no-signal cells are shown separately so that missing information is not mistaken for an actual change.

The main benefit is that it gives people another way to explore Earth data. NASA visualizations are valuable, but not everyone experiences visual information in the same way. EarthPulse is designed with blind and low-vision users in mind, and it may also be useful for anyone who wants to explore data through sound. It has not yet been formally tested with blind or low-vision users.

The project’s intended impact is to make Earth-data exploration more inclusive without replacing the original NASA visualization. The map remains visible while the sound provides an additional layer of information.

We built EarthPulse with React, TypeScript and Vite. The Web Audio API generates the tones directly in the browser, while Python and image-processing tools were used offline to prepare the qualitative grid and optimized visualization assets. The project runs in a web browser and does not require special hardware or a backend.

The creative idea behind EarthPulse is to make the visualization’s legend audible. Instead of adding background music, the project creates a consistent relationship between each visual state and its sound. The same state always produces the same type of tone, while silence indicates that there is no reliable signal to sonify.

During development, we focused on accessibility, scientific honesty, clarity and reproducibility. We avoided presenting the rendered visual classifications as measurements of radiance, brightness, population or geographic change. We also considered how to handle NASA’s regional insets, how to prevent overlapping sounds, how to require user interaction before audio begins and how to clearly explain the source and limitations of the project.
